claims.text: The preserved source establishes even-versus-odd occurrence structure and XOR relevance but does not preserve an exact count of odd-frequency targets.
Under explicit exactly-one or exactly-two target contracts, the candidate XOR cancellation and set-bit partition algorithms recover the target value or values.

When the number of odd-frequency values is unconstrained, a single aggregate XOR is insufficient to identify all members; the candidate therefore does not extend the two-target method without additional state or assumptions.

The executable fixture verifies one/two-target behavior across positive and negative ints, Integer.MIN_VALUE and zero bit patterns, plus explicit null rejection and an impossible xor==0 condition under the exactly-two-distinct-target contract.

findings: The preserved source says that most values occur an even number of times and a minority occur an odd number of times, but it does not preserve whether the odd-frequency target count is exactly one, exactly two, or variable. The candidate keeps that ambiguity explicit instead of silently selecting one classic problem statement.

For an exactly-one target contract, the XOR reduction is correct because equal values occurring an even number of times cancel under associative and commutative XOR, leaving the sole odd-frequency value.

For an exactly-two-distinct-target contract, the total XOR is a^b and is nonzero; selecting a set bit via xor & -xor separates a and b while every repeated value stays wholly in one partition, so partition-local XOR recovers the two targets.

The candidate correctly does not claim that aggregate XOR can recover an arbitrary number of odd-frequency values. It explicitly directs an unconstrained multi-target version to a frequency map or additional structure, preserving the information-sufficiency boundary.

The displayed Java is a complete compilable class matching the separately executed implementation. The deterministic fixture passes positive, negative, zero and Integer.MIN_VALUE bit-pattern cases for one/two-target contracts, plus null rejection and an xor==0 two-target contract-violation case.

The xor==0 check is only a fail-fast necessary-condition check for the exactly-two contract, not a complete proof that arbitrary input contains exactly two odd-frequency values. The answer does not overstate it as complete validation and separately recommends validating the data contract for untrusted input.

Mechanism, complexity, boundary discussion and follow-ups are directly tied to the source question; no personal production experience or unpreserved target-count constraint is fabricated. No coding hard failure or semantic blocker remains for the candidate stage.
